newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Striking truckers tighten grip on Spain.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Striking truckers tighten grip on Spain.

text.p: A truck drivers strike tightened its stranglehold on the Spanish economy as it entered its second week on Thursday and tensions escalated after a French trucker ran over and killed a picket.
The eight-day-old strike to demand improved labour conditions has throttled roads in almost all of northern Spain, cut off supplies to many areas and forced factories to shut.
Unions warned the chaos would spread south.
Strikers blocked a number of main roads and petrol stations and lined their trucks along the hard shoulder of others, intimidating Spanish and foreign drivers who dared to pass.
A picket was run over and killed early on Thursday when he ran into the road to stop a French trucker from passing. The incident in the Burgos region was the most serious so far.
Truckers also blocked border crossings and six northern ports. Hundreds of foreign truckers found themselves caught up in the jam.
The Interior Ministry ordered security forces to guarantee essential supplies to towns. The ministry was due to hold an emergency meeting on Thursday.
The strike has turned violent in some areas.

One driver was slightly injured on Wednesday when he was hit on the head by a stone while trying to fill up his truck at a petrol station in the Leon province. Pickets were also injured in clashes with police.
With the strike blocking supplies to many northern towns, companies were forced to halt production and send workers home.
Car manufacturers were worst hit. Renault's Spanish unit FASA-Renault said it would stop production on Thursday at plants in Valladolid and Palencia.
In the Basque region, France's Michelin was down to half capacity on Wednesday and said it would be paralysed from Thursday if the strike continued.

German producer Mercedez-Benz shut its plants in Barcelona on Wednesday, while production at General Motors unit Opel in Aragon, France's Citroen in Vigo and Nissan in Barcelona also ceased on Thursday.
Other companies including Firestone, Campofrio, and Asturiana del Zinc said they had also been disrupted by a lack of supplies.

Fedatrans, the transport union leading the strike, warned the chaos would worsen and said it had brought another leading union on board, Fenadismer. Others were mulling a call to workers to take action.
In a mimic of the French truckers strike last year which disrupted much of Western Europe with a 12-day blockade, Spanish drivers are demanding a revamp of their sector.
In addition to reducing the retirement age to 60 years from 65, drivers are pushing for diesel subsidies and a revision of tariffs.
Fedatrans said on Wednesday the strike would escalate unless the governement agreed swiftly to their demands.
"To find a solution to this conflict, the Cabinet must meet and approve the measures we are asking for," said Fedatrans spokesman Jon Mikel Abellanal.
The government said it was open to dialogue.
"It is absolutely vital that we sit down together at the negotiation table to resolve the problems in a sector which has many problems," Development Minister Rafael Arias Solgado said.
The French government conceded to drivers' demands during last year's strike which included retirement at 55 instead of 60.
